what_its_for: Calcium carbonate is used for two main purposes: (1) as an antacid to quickly relieve heartburn, acid indigestion, and upset stomach by neutralizing excess stomach acid, and (2) as a calcium supplement to prevent or treat low calcium levels in the body, which helps keep your bones, teeth, heart, and muscles healthy.
how_to_take: Take calcium carbonate exactly as directed on the package or as told by your doctor or pharmacist. If using it as an antacid, chew the chewable tablets thoroughly before swallowing — do not swallow them whole. If using it as a calcium supplement, take it with a full glass of water (8 ounces). For best absorption, take supplement doses with food. Do not take more than the recommended amount at one time or in one day.
dosing: Dosing depends on why you are taking this medicine. As an antacid: adults typically take 500–1,500 mg (1–3 regular-strength Tums) as needed when symptoms occur, up to a maximum of about 7,500 mg per day. Do not use for more than 2 weeks in a row without talking to your doctor. As a calcium supplement: typical adult doses range from 500–1,200 mg of calcium per day, split into 2–3 smaller doses throughout the day for better absorption. Your doctor will tell you the right dose for you. Children's doses are lower — always follow package instructions or ask your pharmacist.
missed_dose: If you are taking calcium carbonate as an antacid, you only take it when you have symptoms, so there is no scheduled dose to miss. If you are taking it as a regular calcium supplement and you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store calcium carbonate at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C–25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Check the expiration date on the package and do not use expired medicine. Dispose of unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist how.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking calcium carbonate within 1–2 hours of taking other medicines, as it can interfere with how your body absorbs many medications, including antibiotics (like tetracycline or ciprofloxacin), thyroid medicine (levothyroxine), iron supplements, and bisphosphonates (like alendronate). Avoid drinking large amounts of milk or eating a lot of dairy products while taking calcium carbonate, as this combination can rarely cause a condition called milk-alkali syndrome. Avoid taking more than the recommended daily amount. If you are on a low-calcium or low-sodium diet, talk to your doctor before using.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek medical help right away if you experience: severe stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting; loss of appetite; unusual tiredness or weakness; muscle pain or weakness; confusion or mood changes; frequent urge to urinate or decreased urination; bone or joint pain; signs of high calcium levels such as excessive thirst, headache, or feeling very drowsy; or if your heartburn or acid symptoms do not improve after 2 weeks of using this medicine. Also call your doctor if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or have kidney disease, kidney stones, or any other serious health condition before starting this medicine.
when_it_works: As an antacid, calcium carbonate works very quickly — usually within 5 to 15 minutes of taking it to relieve heartburn and indigestion. As a calcium supplement, it works over a longer period of time. You may not feel any immediate difference, but it is helping to build and maintain strong bones. Benefits to bone health are usually seen over months to years of regular use.
special_populations: Older adults (65+): Older adults often need calcium supplements to help prevent osteoporosis and bone fractures. However, kidney function may be reduced with age, so check with your doctor about the right dose. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Calcium needs increase during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Talk to your doctor before taking calcium carbonate to make sure you are taking the right amount. Children: Calcium is important for growing bones. Use only products and doses designed for children, and always follow your pediatrician's advice. Kidney disease patients: Use with caution — calcium carbonate can raise calcium and phosphate levels in the blood, which may be harmful if your kidneys are not working well. Always talk to your doctor first. People with a history of kidney stones: Talk to your doctor before taking calcium supplements, as they may increase the risk of certain types of kidney stones.
